claims.text: A heterogeneous microstructure in Mo-enriched Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr will produce yield strength above 1.2 GPa and room-temperature elongation above 15%.
The proposed alloy will have approximately 10% lower density than equiatomic Hf20Mo20Ta20Ti20Zr20.
Synergistic edge-dislocation glide control and strain-gradient hardening will cause the combined strength and ductility improvement.
Equiatomic Hf20Mo20Ta20Ti20Zr20 is a homogeneous BCC solid solution.
The equiatomic Hf20Mo20Ta20Ti20Zr20 baseline has a density of approximately 10.5 g/cm³.
The equiatomic Hf20Mo20Ta20Ti20Zr20 baseline has a yield strength of approximately 830 MPa.
The equiatomic Hf20Mo20Ta20Ti20Zr20 baseline has less than 5% room-temperature ductility.
High-pressure torsion followed by partial annealing will create a bimodal nanograin and coarse-grain structure in Hf15Mo30Ta15Ti20Zr20.
Mo is lighter than the substituted Hf and Ta and therefore its addition will reduce alloy density.
Limiting Mo to 30 at.% or less will maintain BCC phase stability.
Nanograin regions of 50–200 nm will provide high strength through Hall–Petch strengthening.
Coarse-grain regions of 5–10 μm will improve ductility through strain-gradient hardening and dislocation storage.
Mo will segregate to grain boundaries and enhance edge-dislocation mobility.
Edge dislocations control deformation or strength in NbTaTiV and CrMoNbV refractory HEAs.
Edge dislocations will dominate room-temperature plasticity in Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr.
Local stress concentrations in the heterogeneous microstructure will promote wavy dislocation motion and suppress brittle fracture.
Mo substitution will preserve lattice distortion and associated solid-solution strengthening.
The processed alloy will reach a density of no more than 9.5 g/cm³.
Mo contents above 30 at.% will cause Laves-phase formation and catastrophic embrittlement.
Annealing below 1000 K is necessary to prevent detrimental grain coarsening.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis attributes the target properties to processing-induced heterogeneity, but the stated falsification experiment tests only a homogeneous alloy. Poor performance of that homogeneous specimen would not contradict the prediction for the heterogeneous specimen.
